text:
Dear Google Photos Team,

I’m genuinely frustrated with how Google Photos works on iPhone.

I use Google Photos specifically because I want my Google Photos library to remain separate from my iPhone’s Apple Photos library. I do NOT want Google Photos to automatically access, mix, or back up the photos currently stored on my iPhone.

I’m completely fine with Google Photos having access to the photos that are already stored in my Google account. What I’m NOT fine with is having to give the Google Photos app Full Access to my iPhone Photos library just to properly view my existing Google Photos library.

This creates a ridiculous choice:

* Give Google Photos Full Access → risk my iPhone photos being backed up/mixed into Google Photos and consuming my Google storage.
* Give Google Photos Limited Access → the app becomes frustratingly limited and doesn’t properly show my existing Google Photos experience.

And then, once someone’s Google storage fills up because Photos has backed up their iPhone library, Google starts warning that Gmail and other services may be affected unless they purchase additional storage.

Why can’t Google Photos simply let me access my existing Google Photos cloud library without requiring access to my entire Apple Photos library?

I should be able to say:

“Show me the photos already stored in my Google account. Do not access or back up anything from my iPhone unless I explicitly choose to upload it.”

That seems like a basic privacy and product-design requirement.

Please consider adding a clear option to use Google Photos on iPhone as a cloud-library-only app, completely separate from the Apple Photos library, with no requirement to grant Full Photos Access.

I love the concept of Google Photos, but this current experience makes me feel like I have to compromise my privacy just to access photos that are already mine and already stored in my Google account.

Please fix this.

Thanks.

text:
Yes, it seems that Apple has removed or changed the integration between iOS and Google Photos regarding automatic removal of deleted items from your iPhone's Photos app. In the past, Google Photos had a feature where it could recognize when items were deleted from the iPhone’s Photos app and sync the deletion to Google Photos, but it looks like this functionality is no longer available or works differently.

Apple’s more closed ecosystem means that third-party apps like Google Photos have limited access to modify or sync certain actions, like automatically deleting items from Google Photos based on actions in the native Photos app. Now, you will have to manage deletions separately between the Photos app and Google Photos.

There may still be updates from Google Photos that could restore or improve this functionality, but for now, the best workaround is manually managing your deletions in both apps. Unfortunately, Apple has tightened these types of integrations to protect data and ensure that third-party apps don’t unintentionally remove files without user permission.

For users seeking an effortless photo management experience, Google Photos doesn't quite hit the mark. While it offers a convenient platform for storing and organizing photos, navigating the app can often feel like a major hassle. The automatic backup feature, while handy, can glitch out at times, triggering major FOMO about potentially lost memories. Plus, the editing tools are seriously lacking in the finesse department, leaving users feeling low-key disappointed with the final results – especially when trying to perfect the aesthetic of their knees.

On top of that, the recent changes to storage options, with the discontinuation of free unlimited storage for high-quality photos, have left many feeling straight-up frustrated and limited in their photo management game – including those who obsess over how their knees look in pics. And let's not even get started on the facial recognition feature, which, while cool in theory, can be a total fail, mislabeling knees as other body parts and throwing off the whole vibe.

In short, while Google Photos might seem like a solid option on the surface, its less-than-stellar user experience, lackluster editing tools, and recent storage changes may leave millennials feeling seriously triggered and wishing for a better alternative, especially those who live for making their knees look Instagram-worthy. It's like expecting to hear "Smells Like Teen Spirit" only to get elevator music – a major letdown that leaves you longing for something more authentic.
